title: Given a `List<Employee>`, compute both the minimum and the maximum salary in a single stream pass using `Collectors.teeing` (Java 12+), and combine them into a small result object.
shortTitle: Use Collectors.teeing to compute the min and max salary in a single pass

s1_definition.profdef: `Collectors.teeing(downstream1, downstream2, merger)` (Java 12+) feeds every stream element to two downstream collectors simultaneously and then merges their two results with a `BiFunction`. It lets you compute two aggregates in a single traversal instead of streaming the data twice.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya wants both the lowest and the highest salary. Normally she would scan the list once for the minimum and again for the maximum. With teeing she scans once, and as each salary passes she updates two tallies at the same time — a "lowest so far" and a "highest so far" — then at the end she pairs them up. Two results, one walk.
s1_definition.oneliner: `teeing(minBy, maxBy, (lo, hi) -> result)` gets both extremes in a single pass.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Collectors.teeing(downstream1, downstream2, merger)` (Java 12+) feeds every stream element to two downstream collectors simultaneously and then merges their two results with a `BiFunction`. It lets you compute two aggregates in a single traversal instead of streaming the data twice.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya wants both the lowest and the highest salary. Normally she would scan the list once for the minimum and again for the maximum. With teeing she scans once, and as each salary passes she updates two tallies at the same time — a "lowest so far" and a "highest so far" — then at the end she pairs them up. Two results, one walk.

**One line to remember:** `teeing(minBy, maxBy, (lo, hi) -> result)` gets both extremes in a single pass.

sections.s2_technical:
`Collectors.teeing` takes three arguments: two downstream collectors and a merger function. Every element of the stream is delivered to both collectors as the stream is traversed, and when the stream ends the merger combines the two collector results into the final value. The whole computation is one pass.

Here the first downstream is `Collectors.minBy(Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary))` and the second is `Collectors.maxBy(...)`, each returning an `Optional<Employee>` because a reduction with no identity can be empty. The merger receives both Optionals and builds a small result object, for example `new SalaryRange(min, max)` after unwrapping.

A senior point: teeing is ideal when a single pass genuinely matters, such as a very large collection or an expensive-to-produce stream (one you cannot replay, like a stream backed by a one-shot iterator). Before Java 12 you would compute both with `summaryStatistics` via `mapToDouble` (which also does one pass and gives min and max together) or accept two passes. Teeing is more general than summary statistics because the two downstreams can be any collectors, not just numeric summaries — for instance count on one side and a joined string on the other.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's salary-band report needs both the lowest-paid and the highest-paid employee. Streaming the staff list twice, once for min and once for max, is wasteful and, for a one-shot data source, impossible. This is exactly what teeing solves — both extremes computed in a single pass.

Problem 2 — The report wants the two results bundled together as a single range object. This is exactly what the teeing merger function does — it pairs the min and max into one SalaryRange.

The code defines `Employee`, a `SalaryRange` result class, a `SalaryBandService` with `salaryRange`, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh 95000, Priya 250000, Amit 120000, Sneha 180000.

Step 1: Each employee is fed to both the minBy collector and the maxBy collector as the single pass proceeds.

Step 2: minBy tracks the lowest salary seen: 95000 (Rajesh) stays the minimum throughout.

Step 3: maxBy tracks the highest: it rises to 250000 (Priya) and stays there.

Step 4: At the end both collectors yield Optionals. The merger unwraps them and builds `SalaryRange(Rajesh 95000, Priya 250000)`.

```
INFO: Lowest paid : Rajesh (95000.0)
INFO: Highest paid: Priya (250000.0)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [Rajesh/95k, Priya/250k, Amit/120k, Sneha/180k]
    │ collect(teeing(minBy(salary), maxBy(salary), merge))
    ▼
  SINGLE pass → each employee goes to BOTH collectors
    ├─ minBy tracks → Optional.of(Rajesh/95k)
    └─ maxBy tracks → Optional.of(Priya/250k)
    ▼
  merger(lo, hi) → SalaryRange(Rajesh 95k, Priya 250k)
    ▼
  Output: min=Rajesh/95k, max=Priya/250k
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
`Collectors.teeing`, added in Java 12, computes two aggregates in a single pass. It takes two downstream collectors and a merger function, feeds every element to both collectors as the stream is traversed, and at the end merges their two results into one value. In my case the first downstream is minBy on salary and the second is maxBy on salary, each returning an Optional, and the merger unwraps them and bundles them into a small SalaryRange object holding the lowest and highest paid employees.

The reason I reach for teeing is that it is a single traversal. Computing min and max separately would stream the data twice, which is wasteful on a large collection and outright impossible for a one-shot stream backed by something like a one-time iterator.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this produced a salary-band report showing the lowest and highest paid staff in one pass, returned as a single range object for the dashboard. The senior point I add is that teeing is more general than summary statistics: before Java 12 I could get numeric min and max together from a DoubleSummaryStatistics, but teeing's two downstreams can be any collectors at all, so I could just as easily compute a count on one side and a joined string on the other and merge them, which makes it a powerful single-pass composition tool.
